      TARGA RESOURCES LLC’S COMMENTS AND PROPOSED REDLINES IN

TO THE HONORABLE PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION OF TEXAS:

        COMES NOW Targa Resources LLC (Targa) and files these comments and proposed

redlines in response to the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (Commission) Proposal for

Publication of 16 Texas Administrative Code (TAC) § 25.194 (PFP) and respectfully shows as

follows:

                                    I.       INTRODUCTION

        Targa is a leading U.S. midstream energy company that owns, operates, and develops

critical natural gas gathering, processing, and fractionation infrastructure across the Electric

Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT) footprint. Targa has significant operations in the Permian

Basin and a number of large load interconnection requests pending with Oncor Electric Delivery

Company LLC and ERCOT for natural gas processing plants that will be directly affected by the

Commission’s PFP and ERCOT’s Planning Guide Revision Request 145 (PGRR145), Batch Zero

Process for Large Load Interconnections. Targa appreciates the recognition by Commissioner

Hjaltman of the wide-reaching effect of this rule on all types of large loads in Texas, including

critical oil and gas loads. 1

https://www.adminmonitor.com/tx/puct/open_meeting/20260312/ (March 12 Open Meeting).

        Targa has operated in the Permian Basin for many years. Its business focuses on the

efficient and safe delivery of natural gas and natural gas liquids to meet increasing domestic and

global demand for cleaner, affordable fuel and feedstocks, and a significant amount of Targa’s

loads in the Permian Basin region are classified as critical loads under the Public Utility Regulatory

Act (PURA) and the Texas Natural Resources Code. 2 Accordingly, Targa urges the Commission

to carefully consider how the PFP and the PGRR145 process will impact the energization of

longstanding critical large loads. Targa and other oil and gas operators in the Permian Basin have

long suffered from a lack of available grid power in the region, and Targa supported the Permian

Basin Reliability Plan which was adopted by the Commission in PUC Project No. 55718,

Reliability Plan for the Permian Basin Under PURA § 39.167 and promulgated pursuant to Texas

House Bill 5066.

       As a threshold matter, Targa urges the Commission to clarify that critical loads will be

treated as firm load in ERCOT’s Batch 0, as well as in future batch runs. Targa appreciates that

ERCOT’s April 4 comments in PGRR145 added that the Permian Basin Reliability Plan (PBRP)

Study completed by ERCOT in 2024 will be considered a “complete and valid” study for its batch

zero large load evaluation and firm load consideration. 3 However, the PBRP study did not specify

all oil and gas loads seeking interconnection in the Permian Basin so this modification alone may

not be sufficient to capture load that supported the plan. Accordingly, the Commission should

clarify how loads not specifically modeled in the PBRP study will be considered firm in the batch

zero process. Targa further requests that the Commission ensure that critical loads be treated as

firm load in future batch runs. Further, if the Transmission and Distribution Service Providers

       Targa’s comments address the following key areas: protection of competitively sensitive

information; the appropriateness of site-related study and regulatory approval disclosures at the

Intermediate Agreement phase; the level and refundability of financial security; CIAC payment

structure and refundability; the 80/20 forfeiture framework for withdrawal and non-utilized

specific proposals are set forth in the Executive Summary appended to these comments and in the

redline edits attached as Appendix A.

       Essentially, the final large load interconnection rule should ensure a workable, transparent,

and reliable process for large load interconnections that are essential to maintaining service to

critical natural gas infrastructure that supports the ERCOT system and the Texas economy. In

consistent with the organization of the PFP, as prescribed by the Commission. 6 The Commission

required interested persons to file comments by April 17, 2026. 7 Therefore, these comments are

                  II.       COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR PUBLICATION

       Targa appreciates the consideration Commission Staff has provided to allow the

Commission to put forward this PFP. However, the current proposal tends to create an overly rigid

regulatory scheme that does not account for the commercial complexities and grid energization

uncertainty inherent in large scale project developments in ERCOT, including development of

natural gas processing facilities or traditional large manufacturing facilities. To account for these

complexities, Targa has proposed several revisions that would allow for large load development

to flourish in Texas while balancing the policy objective that costs to all utility customers remain

reasonable.

       Overall, Targa favors an approach that would impose gradual, refundable financial burdens

on large load customers early in the interconnection process, that would become hard

commitments as the project obtains certainty that it can energize and execute an interconnection

agreement. This approach will account for the financial and developmental complexities of large

loads and ensure reliable access to power for all ERCOT customers.

A.     Competitively Sensitive Information

       Under the PFP, the Commission defines “Competitively Sensitive Information” with

substantial exceptions for large swaths of personal and operational data:

       Competitively sensitive information includes exact site locations, such as parcel
       identifiers or property boundaries; commercial terms, such as pricing or internal
       development prioritization; proprietary architectural, operational, or compute-
       deployment strategies; and financing structures.        Competitively sensitive
       information does not include the identity of a large load customer; general site
       location, such as load zone; requested or contracted peak demand; timing of
       energization; or whether an interconnection request is associated with the
       same applicant or affiliated entities. 8


           8
               PFP at 7-8 (Proposed 16 TAC § 25.194(c)(2)) (emphasis added).
                                                       7
        The exceptions in this definition for competitively sensitive information are overly broad

and would allow parties to receive commercially sensitive nonpublic information that could be

used by other competitors to reverse engineer project ownership, locations, construction timelines,

and size long before a project is built. The oil and gas industry is highly competitive and requiring

large loads to publicly file details about their projects years before they are constructed would

cause competitive harm. The Texas Public Information Act (TPIA) excepts from disclosure

“commercial or financial information for which it is demonstrated based on specific factual

evidence that disclosure would cause substantial competitive harm to the person from whom the

information was obtained,” unless the information contains certain information regarding contracts

between governmental entities and their vendors and contractors. 9 Under the PFP, information

like the specific identity of the large load, site location, peak demand, and anticipated energization

date would allow competitors to have a substantial advantage to determine where new oil and gas

facilities are sited and reverse engineer the capacity and scale of these new operations. Public

disclosure of this information would cause competitive harm to Targa and other large oil and gas

loads, in violation of the TPIA. Targa urges the Commission to narrow the exceptions to the

definition of publicly sensitive information to exclude the disclosure of commercially sensitive

information that would be excluded from disclosure under the TPIA.

       The PFP also allows ERCOT to demand “any competitively sensitive information” it

“deems necessary to complete any analysis required as part of the interconnection process.” 10 This

language does not require ERCOT’s request to be reasonably related to the interconnection

process.   Therefore, ERCOT could request competitively sensitive information that has no

operational details, or other proprietary organizational information. Targa supports the need for

ERCOT to have all the information necessary to conduct its interconnection studies, however,

requiring ERCOT to demonstrate a nexus between the information requested and the specific

interconnection study will provide reasonable guardrails and limit the disclosure of commercially

sensitive information.

B.      Site Control

        Targa supports the change made by the Commission during its March 12, 2026 open

meeting to allow large load customers to demonstrate site control through a signed and executed

option to purchase or lease the real property for the customer’s planned facilities. 11 As Chairman

Gleeson noted, options to lease or buy are “common tools used by developers to secure site control

. . . while minimizing financial risks.” 12 Without this change, large loads would need to make

unnecessary financial commitments early on in the batch study process before any party has a clear

picture about the costs and types of electrical facilities required to serve the projects. In practice,

the substantial growth of large loads and the corresponding extended timelines for TDSPs to

deliver electric service are a primary reason developers rely on option agreements to maintain site

control to avoid committing resources to leases and sales years before the project may come online.

Targa supports this inclusion and recommends the Commission adopt this provision in its final

rule.

 C.       Site-Related Studies and Regulatory Approvals

         1.          Site-Related Studies and Regulatory Approvals at the Intermediate Agreement

                     Phase

         The PFP requires large load customers to submit to its interconnecting Transmission

Service Provider (TSP) and/or Distribution Service Provider (DSP) the customer’s plans, expected

timing, and progress for site-related studies and engineering services as part of its Intermediate

Agreement. 13 While the PFP already requires this submission to be accompanied by an officer

attestation that the information is complete and accurate, Targa’s concern is that the underlying

requirement to submit detailed plans and studies—such as geotechnical surveys, water use, and

gas supply information—goes beyond what is necessary at this stage and beyond the ability of the

utilities and ERCOT to appropriately analyze. 14 Much of this information has limited relevance

to the interconnection itself and will not impact ERCOT’s ability to conduct any interconnection

study for potential projects. If this information were publicly disclosed, it would commercially

harm large load customers, especially oil and gas loads, whose geotechnical studies and site

development plans constitute proprietary nonpublic information that, if disclosed, would provide

competitors a significant competitive advantage. 15 Accordingly, Targa proposes that the officer

attestation alone—without submission of the underlying plans, studies, or permit applications—

should suffice at the Intermediate Agreement phase. This approach would still demonstrate the

       The PFP also requires large load customers to submit plans, expected timing, and current

        2.          Quarterly Reporting Requirements

       In addition to the initial provision of information on Site-Related Studies and Regulatory

Approvals, the PFP requires large load customers to provide updates and progress reports on this

information “when requested” 18 by the interconnecting TSP or DSP, at a frequency of no more

than quarterly. While the PFP frames this as an on-request obligation rather than a mandatory

quarterly filing, the provision nonetheless creates a mechanism by which TSPs and DSPs could

demand up to four reporting cycles per year for information that has limited relevance to the

interconnection process itself. These reporting demands are particularly burdensome during the

Intermediate Agreement phase when the project is in the earlier stages of development and site-

related studies may not yet have commenced. Targa requests the removal of these reporting

requirements, which create unnecessary regulatory burden for large loads without providing

commensurate benefit to TSPs, DSPs, and ERCOT.

D.     Financial Security

       1.          Non-Refundability

       Targa appreciates the Commission’s change from its initial $100,000/MW proposal for a

required financial security to $50,000/MW in the PFP. 19 However, while this security amount

appears reasonable, the Commission’s final rule should adopt additional refundability provisions

that do not penalize large loads for withdrawing projects early on during development. Once a

project reaches the Interconnection Agreement phase, the PFP requires the large load customer to

pay a separate non-refundable interconnection fee of $50,000 per MW of contracted peak demand.

While the PFP provides that any unused financial security posted at the Intermediate Agreement

a customer’s requested load or may not grant that request in a timely manner, designating this fee

The PFP already has refundability provisions for other interconnection costs that allow large load

customers to recoup some costs if a project ultimately withdraws. 21 Accordingly, the final rule

should apply similar cost-causation principles to allow portions of the interconnection fee to be

refundable.

        2.          Parent Guaranty

        At the interconnection agreement phase, the PFP allows large load customers to use a

phase. 24 Targa supports the optionality that providing parent guaranties provides and urges their

inclusion in the final rule. Allowing for parent guarantees recognizes the current business practices

for most utilities and will support growth by credit worthy large loads.

 E.     CIAC Payment Timing and Refundability

       1.          Initial CIAC Payments

       At the time the Interconnection Agreement is executed, the PFP requires large load

customers to pay “all direct interconnection costs” through contribution in aid of construction

(CIAC) payments. 25 Requiring the full payment of all interconnection costs at the time the

interconnection agreement is executed misaligns the assignment of construction costs and puts an

unreasonable burden on large load customers before construction even begins. This burden is

especially acute for smaller large loads when interconnection costs make up a larger proportion of

the customer’s budget. At the March 12 open meeting, Chairman Gleeson noted the possibility of

gradual, progressive escalators throughout the large load interconnection process as a reasonable

compromise between large loads and TSPs. 26                  Implementing a graduated, phased payment

structure based on construction milestones represents a reasonable approach that does not require

substantial upfront payments by large loads before construction even begins.

       2.          True-Ups

       Under the PFP, overpayment of interconnection costs by a large load customer are only

repaid gradually by TSPs through bill credits rather than full upfront payments to customers.27

Essentially, TSPs are only required to pay back overestimated CIAC through incremental losses

to revenue rather than actual one-time payments to customers. Such a system incentivizes TSPs

to overestimate CIAC payments because they will receive full payment for the estimated amount

upfront and then will only pay back excess costs incrementally through bill credits, potentially

requiring a one-time direct repayment of any overestimated CIAC costs to the large load customer

upon completion of all direct interconnection facilities.

       3.          Refunds on Cancellation

       Under the current proposal, all CIAC funds paid by the customer are flatly non-

refundable. 28 Such a scheme represents a windfall for TSPs, who will be able to keep all CIAC

funds if a customer withdraws its project without any limitations. CIAC payments are intended to

make the interconnecting utility whole for actual costs incurred—not to create a revenue stream.

Historically, CIACs for cancelled projects have been refundable less the actual costs expended by

the utility. Accordingly, Targa recommends that the final rule implement a refund procedure

whereby the customer will be refunded any CIAC funds not already expended by the TSP at the

time the customer provides notice of the project’s withdrawal.

F.     Financial Security Forfeiture

       1.          80% Forfeiture Upon Withdrawal

       Upon the withdrawal of a portion of the requested peak demand of a large load project,

only 20% of the balance of any outstanding funds are refunded to customers and 80% of the funds

are kept by the interconnecting TSP as an offset to the TSP’s rate base. 29 This same 80/20 split

also applies to non-utilized capacity. 30 These provisions would give interconnecting TSPs a

windfall of funds supplied by large load customers with no direct connection to used and useful

80% of these funds does not align the utility’s costs with the assets it has placed in service for the

benefit of ratepayers, contrary to general cost-causation principles of utility ratemaking. The 80%

forfeiture provision effectively converts what should be a cost-recovery mechanism into a revenue

stream for interconnecting utilities, untethered from actual costs incurred. Targa recommends

allowing large load customers to retain 100% of the funds remaining after applying the financial

security to any outstanding amounts owed, which would leave interconnecting TSPs and DSPs

whole without imposing punitive forfeitures on customers.

         2.          5-Year Holding Period

         Under the PFP, interconnecting entities are only required to refund any remaining financial

security for projects that have sustained operations for five years at the customer’s contracted peak

demand. 32 This extended holding period is not reasonably tied to the provision of electrical

services. For large loads under 250 MW that do not necessitate significant systemwide upgrades,

there is no reasonable justification for any holding period once the project has reached its

contracted peak demand, and all remaining funds should be refundable immediately. Allowing

potentially millions of dollars to remain tied to a specific facility for years after it has achieved

commercial operation hinders economic development by raising barriers to entry. While a shorter

holding period may be warranted for larger projects to confirm the large load customer has

achieved full commercial operation, requiring utilities to hold security for five years for smaller

projects after it reaches its contracted peak demand effectively transforms the utility into a

         3.          Equipment Costs

         In addition to traditional stranded assets, customers who withdraw or do not reach their

requested peak demand are also required to pay the full costs of “equipment” that the

interconnecting entity procured and cannot return with a full refund. 34 Such a proposal runs

any cost to the customer. However, in the rare instance that the utility cannot use the equipment

G.      Non-Utilized Capacity and Clawback

        The PFP stipulates that missing a proposed milestone for phased energization by six

months triggers an automatic security forfeiture under the 80/20 rule described above and requires

ERCOT to reallocate non-utilized capacity. 38 This rule is too rigid and does not reflect the

complexities of many large load projects that could be delayed for any number of reasons beyond

their control such as geopolitical conflicts or supply chain issues. Moreover, the PFP creates a

fundamental asymmetry: while large load customers face strict timelines and severe financial

penalties for failing to meet phased energization milestones, TDSPs face no corresponding

obligation to complete interconnection facilities and deliver service within a specified timeframe.

Penalizing large load customers for delays that may result from the TDSP’s own performance is

inequitable and contrary to sound regulatory policy. Targa appreciates the concerns related to

stranded assets and the need to reallocate non-utilized capacity. However, extending the deadline

for missing a phased energization to 18 months represents a reasonable proposal that accounts for

the complexities of large-scale economic developments and the uncertainty in TDSP delivery

timelines. Further, creating an automatic reallocation of all non-utilized capacity in the rule does

not allow TSPs, large load customers, and ERCOT to reach equitable solutions in the event of a

       Targa appreciates the consideration Commission Staff has provided to allow the
